analysis.investment_thesis: Chalet Hotels is riding India's premium hospitality upcycle with EBITDA margins of ~44% and operating cash flow surging to INR 950 Cr in FY25, but an aggressive capex cycle (INR 969 Cr in FY25) has turned FCF negative and suppressed net profit to INR 142 Cr despite revenue of INR 1,718 Cr. The India travel-and-leisure structural tailwind is real, but the capital intensity and low ROE of 5.77% make this a marginal Fisher candidate.
key_strengths: Operating CF compounding strongly: INR 62 Cr (FY22) → INR 950 Cr (FY25), demonstrating real asset productivity
Operating margins of 35.5% and EBITDA margins ~44% reflect genuine pricing power in premium urban locations
Revenue CAGR of 12.8% over 9 years with clear post-COVID acceleration (INR 508 Cr FY22 → INR 1,718 Cr FY25)
key_risks: ROE of only 5.77% is far below my 20% threshold — capital is not being deployed efficiently despite strong margins
Debt/Equity of 0.73 exceeds my 0.5 comfort level; total debt remains INR 2,604 Cr even after recent equity raise
Net profit fell sharply from INR 278 Cr (FY24) to INR 142 Cr (FY25) as depreciation and finance costs absorbed revenue growth
red_flags: Free cash flow turned negative in FY25 at -INR 14 Cr due to capex surge of INR 969 Cr — growth is not yet self-funding
Net profit trajectory is erratic (losses in 5 of 9 years), indicating vulnerability to cyclical downturns
Heavy equity dilution in FY25 (reserves nearly doubled to INR 3,196 Cr) signals reliance on external capital for growth
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Chalet operates premium hotels in high-barrier metro markets — Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru — which provides some locational moat and justifies strong EBITDA margins. The post-COVID recovery has been impressive, with revenue nearly tripling from FY22 troughs, and operating cash flows now covering interest costs comfortably. However, I look for businesses that compound wealth through returns on reinvested capital, not just asset appreciation, and a 5.77% ROE tells me the hotel real estate model is inherently capital-hungry with modest equity returns.

The FY25 capex surge of INR 969 Cr — more than 4x the prior year — signals management is investing aggressively in new capacity. This could be visionary if India's premium hotel supply remains constrained, but the simultaneous decline in net profit and negative FCF in FY25 give me pause. I want to see this new capacity generating returns before committing fully; the story needs 2–3 years of proof.
